solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Acquisitive chap, as we see it

parts.note: cove is old British slang for a man or fellow
to us, meaning in our view

explanation.surface: A grasping man explains things from his own point of view.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone acquisitive is eager to get possessions, which is to be greedy or grasping.

clue.text: Charles's going to loudly show amusement

indicators.note: loudly says the words are to be heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: Chuck is a familiar form of Charles, and Chuck'll is Chuck will

explanation.surface: Charles is about to laugh out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: To laugh quietly is a way to show amusement.

clue.text: Number one Scot with puritanical views

parts.note: the victor is the winner, the number one
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: The top Scot holds strict moral opinions.
explanation.definitionFit: The era of Queen Victoria is associated with prim, strict moral attitudes.

clue.text: What handyman has flipping spoils apparel

indicators.note: flipping means the word for spoils is turned back to front

parts.note: loot is plunder or spoils
kit is clothing or gear, as in football kit

explanation.surface: A handyman's ruined clothing gets damned spoiled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British swearword but signals a turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: A handyman carries a set of tools for jobs, his equipment bag.

clue.text: Errant knight in huge trouble

indicators.note: errant means wandering astray, so the letters stray into a new order

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A wandering knight finds himself in great difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Errant' sits with 'knight' as in knight errant, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To unhinge someone is to disturb or upset their mind, to trouble them deeply.

clue.text: Back yard fencing weak and sagging

indicators.note: Back tells us to read the whole assembled piece from end to start
fencing means the yard's letters surround, like a fence, the word for weak

parts.note: yd is the standard abbreviation for the unit of length
poor, as in a feeble or weak performance

explanation.surface: A neglected back garden with a feeble, sagging fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reverses the whole assembly, giving YPOORD before the turnaround; 'Back yard' tempts you to read a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagging and drooping both describe something hanging down limply.

clue.text: Turned tenacious, holding on

indicators.note: holding means the tenacious word contains the cricket term

parts.note: dogged means persistent and tenacious
in cricket the on side is also called the leg side

explanation.surface: Someone stubborn turned round, clinging on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' as the cricket side is a convention: on side and leg side are the same half of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog-legged road or hole bends sharply at an angle, so it has turned.

clue.text: Stuff's possibly tax-free, before cuts

definitions.note: the definition is stuff, to gorge oneself; the 's means is

indicators.note: cuts means the word for before slices into the tax piece

parts.note: O VAT, zero value added tax, is what a tax-free item might carry
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: Goods might be free of tax, ahead of spending cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is Britain's value added tax on sales; zero-rated goods carry nought VAT, hence 'possibly tax-free'.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff oneself is to eat far too much, to gorge.

clue.text: Praise, primarily, to give the thing acclaim?

definitions.text: Praise, primarily, to give the thing acclaim?

indicators.note: primarily asks for the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: to laud it is to give the thing praise, with it standing for the thing

explanation.surface: Praise is chiefly a way of honouring something.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: P plus 'laud it' gives an expression of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaudit is an expression of praise or applause.

clue.text: Stripping off uniform, love holding colonel's coat

parts.note: U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: holding means the word for love wraps around the letters that follow

parts.note: love is a score of nothing in tennis

indicators.note: the coat of a word is its outside, so its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone undresses, taking off a uniform while gripping an officer's coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coat' takes only the outside letters of colonel, and tennis scores love as zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Stripping off is taking clothes off, the same as undressing.

clue.text: Without a mark where they should be gained

parts.note: ex is a preposition meaning without or excluding, as in ex dividend
M stands for mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: Someone without a single mark, in the place where marks ought to be earned.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the previous words: 'they' are the marks a candidate tries to win.
explanation.definitionFit: A test is the place where a student hopes to earn marks.

clue.text: Put a stop to Rugby's foul school leader

parts.note: a knock-on is an infringement in rugby when the ball is dropped forward
the Head is the head teacher of a school

explanation.surface: The head teacher of Rugby School halts a foul game.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby is also a famous English school, which tempts the solver to read the clue as about the school rather than the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: To end a plan abruptly is the idiom of knocking it on the head.

clue.text: Foreign letter coming in is the French letter

indicators.note: coming in means the Greek letter enters the French words

parts.note: in French, is is est and the is le
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A letter from abroad arrives, and it turns out to be a condom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French letter' is British slang for a condom, a misdirection; 'coming in' puts PI inside EST after its first letter, then LE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal written message, especially one in the New Testament.

clue.text: One admitted to being unstable? It's still to be settled

indicators.note: admitted to means one is let inside the word for instability

parts.note: lability is the state of being labile, unstable or liable to change
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to being shaky; it's unresolved.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt is something owed and not yet paid off.

clue.text: Charge to pack knick-knacks hurriedly

indicators.note: to pack means the charge word has something stuffed inside it

parts.note: an agio is a charge made for changing money
tat is cheap, tasteless ornaments

explanation.surface: A fee for packing up trinkets in a rush.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitato is a musical direction to play in an agitated, hurried way.

clue.text: This vicar could be the record-holder

indicators.note: could be means these letters might become a different word when rearranged

explanation.surface: A clergyman might be the one who holds the record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record-holder' suggests a sporting champion; here it is someone who keeps records.
explanation.definitionFit: An archivist keeps and looks after historical documents and records.

clue.text: At first, bear one fruit or another

indicators.note: At first asks for only the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: ananas is another name for the pineapple

explanation.surface: A bear eats one kind of fruit or a different one.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads with what goes before: 'another' fruit beside the pineapple.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow tropical fruit is a different fruit from the pineapple, so it is another.

clue.text: Complaint received by a miserly sort presenting a threat to workers

definitions.text: sort presenting a threat to workers

indicators.note: received by means the illness goes inside the miserly word

parts.note: near is a dated British word for mean with money
TB, tuberculosis, is a medical complaint

explanation.surface: A miser catches an illness, endangering his employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'workers' are worker ants, the prey of this animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardvark, also called this, eats ants, so it is a danger to the worker ants.

clue.text: Liberal leader gave up splitting wood

indicators.note: splitting means the gave-up word cuts the wood apart

parts.note: ash is a tree and its timber
quit means stopped or gave up

explanation.surface: A party leader quit chopping logs.
explanation.walkthrough: H. H. Asquith was the British Liberal Prime Minister from 1908 to 1916.
explanation.definitionFit: Asquith led the Liberal Party and the government before and during the First World War.

clue.text: Cited tot defending authoritarian leader

indicators.note: defending means the word for tot surrounds and protects the leader

parts.note: to tot up is to add
Il Duce was the title of Mussolini, the Italian dictator

explanation.surface: A small child is quoted protecting a dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tot' looks like a child but is the verb meaning add up.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence adduced is evidence cited or brought forward in argument.

clue.text: Light vessel reversed by a kingdom once

indicators.note: reversed means the light and vessel pieces are read backwards together

parts.note: airy means light and breezy
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A small ship backed up by a former realm.
explanation.definitionFit: This was an ancient Mesopotamian empire, a realm that no longer exists.

clue.text: Ruling line in colour, almost ugly

indicators.note: almost means the colouring word loses its final letter

parts.note: a dye is a colouring
nasty means unpleasant or ugly, as in an ugly scene

explanation.surface: A royal family dressed in a nearly hideous shade.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynasty is a succession of rulers from one family.

clue.text: European bank invests — diving in here?

indicators.note: invests means the European letter is put inside the bank word

parts.note: to bank on is to depend on

explanation.surface: A European bank makes investments, plunging in headfirst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' looks like a financial institution but is the verb, as in bank on.
explanation.definitionFit: The deepest part of a swimming pool is where people dive in.

clue.text: Heady mixture of qualities nurse developed

indicators.note: developed suggests these letters have been worked into a new form

explanation.surface: A nurse has developed an intoxicating blend of qualities.
explanation.definitionFit: This cocktail of spirit, orange juice and grenadine is an alcoholic mix that goes to the head.

clue.text: A little house might … be this?

indicators.note: A little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A small house might well be a semi-detached one.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis and question mark tie it together: the hidden word is itself a kind of little house.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-detached home is a typical modest British house, so a little house might be one.

clue.text: The writer's twice penning papers of merit

indicators.note: penning means the writer's words enclose the papers like a pen

parts.note: the writer's read twice: once as I'm (the writer is) and once as I've (the writer has)
the press means the newspapers

explanation.surface: A writer twice composes newspaper pieces worth reading.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer's must be expanded two ways, as 'the writer is' and 'the writer has', one each side of the papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something impressive is worthy, a work deserving respect or admiration.

clue.text: Highest-ranking lady has heart stolen roguishly

parts.note: arch as a prefix means chief or highest, as in archbishop

indicators.note: has heart stolen means the two middle letters of lady are taken out

explanation.surface: A grand lady loses her heart to a rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak archly is to be playfully mischievous, cheekily knowing.

clue.text: Grant a leader in the papers a column

parts.note: Cary Grant was the Hollywood film star

indicators.note: leader in asks for the first letter of the following word

parts.note: ID means identity papers

explanation.surface: Someone gives a newspaper editorial its own column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like a verb but is the actor; 'leader' looks like an editorial.
explanation.definitionFit: A caryatid is a pillar carved as a female figure, so a kind of column.
